lens: Adversarial audit for survivorship and selection bias in the zen validation harness (eventstudy.py, trials.py, leak.py, study_volume.py), with every hypothesis tested by running code against the parquet archive and counting rows before and after each step.

findings.line_hint: 113-118 (merge_asof in adjusted_prices), with root cause at 80 (reverse cumprod in adjustment_factors)
findings.problem: When a symbol has TWO corporate actions on the same ex_date (a bonus and a face-value split on the same day is the standard Indian pattern), merge_asof matches each price row to only ONE of them. The reverse cumprod produces one partially-cumulated row and one fully-cumulated row for that date, and which one wins depends on an unstable sort. Prices before the ex-date therefore get the wrong cumulative factor and the adjusted series has a fabricated jump.
findings.evidence:
33 symbol/ex_date pairs carry more than one factor row, across 602 symbols with any factor. Affected list includes BAJFINANCE, BAJAJFINSV, 360ONE, CUPID, NAZARA, EASEMYTRIP, GPIL, LINC, CGCL, VEEDOL.

Printed from es.adjusted_prices(), 'applied' = factor on the last pre-ex row / first post-ex row:
  BAJAJFINSV ex 2022-09-13  correct combined factor 0.1   applied 0.1/1    adjusted move across ex-date   +4.1%   (correct by luck)
  BAJFINANCE ex 2025-06-16  correct combined factor 0.1   applied 0.1/1    adjusted move across ex-date   +0.5%   (correct by luck)
  360ONE     ex 2023-03-02  correct combined factor 0.25  applied 0.5/1    adjusted move across ex-date  -50.3%   FABRICATED
  CUPID      ex 2024-04-04  correct combined factor 0.05  applied 0.1/0.2  adjusted move across ex-date  -89.5%   FABRICATED

360ONE raw close 1773.30 -> 441.05 across a Bonus 1:1 PLUS a 1:2 split (true combined 0.25). Archive says adj_close 886.65 -> 441.05 = -50.3%.
CUPID's factor is 0.008333 on 2018-10-10 and 0.100000 on 2018-10-11, producing a single-session adjusted move of +1002% inside a period with only a 1:5 bonus (raw 203.35 -> 186.10, i.e. -8.5%).

In the vol_x=10 3000-event sample, 30 of 10,684 scored outcomes hold across one of these mis-adjusted dates, including GLOBE +313% at 6m and VERTOZ +279% at 24m (both counted as multibaggers) and SHRENIK -94% at 12m.
findings.why_it_inflates: It manufactures returns of -90% to +1000% out of nothing, in the one function every reported return passes through. The sign is set by an unstable sort, so it is not self-cancelling: half the affected names get a fake multibagger and half a fake wipeout. It hits BAJFINANCE-class names — the compounders that split and bonus repeatedly — which is exactly the population any screen is built to find, so the module's own stated guarantee ('the error lands hardest on exactly the winners a screen is meant to find') is violated by its implementation.
findings.fix: Collapse corpactions to one row per (symbol, ex_date) before computing the cumulative factor: SELECT symbol, ex_date, exp(sum(ln(factor))) AS factor FROM corpactions WHERE factor > 0 AND factor < 1 GROUP BY symbol, ex_date, then reverse-cumprod on that. Add a regression assertion that no symbol/ex_date pair survives with count(*) > 1, and a panel-wide guard that no adjusted single-session move falls outside about -55% to +120% without a matching corporate action.

findings.line_hint: 70-74 (the 'factor IS NOT NULL AND factor > 0 AND factor < 1' filter in adjustment_factors)
findings.problem: The adjustment table silently ignores every share-count-changing action whose factor failed to parse, plus whole classes it cannot represent. Those price breaks are then recorded as genuine returns. The filter also drops factor >= 1 entirely, so consolidations and reverse splits are never adjusted in either direction.
findings.evidence:
Of 25,853 corpaction rows only 831 carry a usable factor. 41 rows that change the share count have a NULL factor; 100 demergers and 284 rights issues cannot be represented by this schema at all. NSE also files face-value splits under action='other' with subjects like 'Fv Splt Frm Rs 10 To Re 1' (VERTOZ, VIJIFIN), which the parser misses.

Raw price moves that survive into adj_close as real returns:
  TRENT      ex 2016-09-12  Rs10->Re1 split, NULL factor, not in adjustment table:  2344.80 -> 241.45  = -89.7%
  GRASIM     ex 2016-10-06  Rs10->Rs2 split, NULL factor:                           4933.55 -> 1009.20 = -79.5%
  KAJARIACER ex 2016-10-04  Rs2->Re1 split, NULL factor:                            1398.55 -> 699.35  = -50.0%
  JMTAUTOLTD ex 2016-09-21  Rs2->Re1 split, NULL factor:                              46.85 -> 25.55   = -45.5%
  AJANTPHARM ex 2022-06-22  Bonus 1:2, NULL factor:                                 1840.80 -> 1214.80 = -34.0%

Actions missing from corpactions entirely: TIPSINDLTD has zero rows and shows -90.4% on 2023-04-21; KAUSHALYA shows +9,933% in one session on 2024-02-06 (an unrecorded consolidation).

Scanning the adjusted panel for the 1,516 symbols in the vol_x=5 sample (3.24M rows): 73 single-session adjusted moves worse than -55% or better than +120%. 71 of 10,763 scored outcome rows hold across one, with median excess return of -87.2% at the 24-month horizon. Excluding them moves the vol_x=5 24m beat rate 37.3% -> 37.8% and median excess -25.1% -> -24.2%.
findings.why_it_inflates: TRENT is one of the decade's largest Indian multibaggers and this archive records it as losing 90% in a single session. Any factor study, any momentum ranking, and any 'what happened to the winners' analysis reads that as a real outcome. The consolidation cases point the other way and fabricate 10x and 100x gains, which flow straight into multibagger_pct and mean_excess_pct. Because 'other' is the second-largest action bucket (9,627 rows) the true miss rate is unknown, so no result from this engine currently carries a bounded adjustment error.
findings.fix: Parse the subject text for face-value changes and ratios regardless of the action label ('Fv Splt', 'Face Value Split', 'Consolidation', 'From Rs X To Rs Y'), and allow factor >= 1 so consolidations adjust. Treat demergers and rights issues as explicit non-adjustable events: flag any holding window spanning one and exclude it with a reported count rather than scoring it. Add the continuity check from finding 1 as a hard gate on the archive, not just the study.

findings.line_hint: 195-219 — target is computed from the horizon and used for the benchmark exit even when the stock exit was forced to sym_last at line 204-208
findings.problem: For a delisted or truncated name the stock is exited at its last traded price (correct), but the benchmark return is still measured from entry to the FULL horizon date. Stock return over 3 days is then compared against an index return over 24 months. This is precisely the benchmark-alignment error the module docstring says it refuses to make.
findings.evidence:
Reproducing baseline() exactly (seed 7, 40 dates, 60 names): 1,176 delisted-and-complete outcome rows, of which 161 were held for less than 90% of the nominal horizon.

  horizon  n   median held days  median stock  median benchmark  median excess
     3    11         43            +5.3%            +4.7%           -0.9%
     6    20         70            +6.2%            +6.8%           -3.6%
    12    47        189            +5.3%            +5.7%           -7.9%
    24    83        307            +2.6%           +27.9%          -25.5%

Worked cases: MINDAIND entered 2022-08-01, exited 2022-08-04 (3 days, renamed to UNOMINDA), stock +3.8%, and at 24m the benchmark is credited +58.3% giving a recorded excess of -54.6%. HERIT-RE has entry_date == exit_date, 0 days held, and is scored 'complete' at all four horizons.

Re-deriving the benchmark over the ACTUAL entry->exit window: random baseline 24m beat rate 41.1% -> 41.8%, median excess -15.3% -> -14.3%; vol_x=5 24m 38.6% -> 39.1%, median excess -20.6% -> -18.6%.
findings.why_it_inflates: Roughly 4% of scored 24-month observations carry a mechanical -25pp median excess that is arithmetic, not market outcome. It currently deflates both arms by similar amounts so it does not overturn the volume conclusion, but it inflates any strategy whose delisted names skew differently from the control, and it makes the reported median_excess and worst_pct columns unusable as levels. It also survives as a landmine for a fundamental screen, where forced exits will not be randomly distributed.
findings.fix: Set the benchmark exit from the actual exit_date, not from target. Also stop reusing one truncated exit price across all four horizons: an event whose stock stopped trading at month 2 has no genuine 24-month outcome and should either be reported as complete=True with an explicit truncated=True flag and a matched benchmark window, or be reinvested into the benchmark from the delisting date, but the same number must never be filed as both the 3-month and the 24-month result.

findings.line_hint: 140-143 (all_dates[::step][:40] feeding es.baseline with n_per_date=60), and eventstudy.py:278-299
findings.problem: The random baseline draws 2,400 observations from only 40 entry dates. Every one of the 60 names picked on a given date shares the same entry, the same benchmark window and the same market regime, so the observations are massively cross-sectionally correlated. Every statistic downstream is quoted as if n = 2,400 independent draws.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced exactly: 'baseline picks: 2400, distinct dates: 40, distinct symbols: 1204'. The signal arm by contrast has 3,000 events on 2,220 distinct dates.

12-month beat rate, shipped baseline = 42.6%
  naive SE assuming 2,220 independent obs:  1.05 pp
  cluster-robust SE over 40 date clusters:  2.07 pp
  per-date beat rate ranges from 18% to 67%

So the '42.6% of random liquid stocks beat Nifty 500' constant carries a 95% interval of roughly 38.5%-46.7%, not 40.5%-44.7%.
findings.why_it_inflates: This is the yardstick every future study will be measured against. A signal reporting a 47% hit rate looks like a clear 4-5pp edge against 42.6% under the naive SE and is inside noise under the correct one. Nothing in the code or the write-up records that the effective sample size is 40, so the next strategy that clears the bar by a few points will be believed. Note I tested the point estimate itself and it holds: a date-matched control drawn on the same 2,220 event dates (9,000 picks) also gives 42.6% at 12m and 42.6%/43.9% at 12m/3m, so the volume conclusion survives — the defect is in the stated precision, not the number.
findings.fix: Draw the control on the SAME dates as the events being tested (a date-matched control), which also removes any period mismatch between arms. Report cluster-robust standard errors clustered on entry date, and print the number of distinct entry dates next to every hit rate. Feed n_obs into deflated_sharpe as the number of independent time clusters, not the number of rows.

findings.line_hint: 71-77 — median(volume) OVER (...) compared against raw `volume` in the WHERE clause at 88-89
findings.problem: find_events compares raw traded share volume against a raw trailing 60-session median with no split or bonus adjustment. A share-count change multiplies volume mechanically, so every split and bonus ex-date manufactures a volume spike of exactly the split ratio. The event sample is contaminated with corporate-action artefacts, concentrated in the highest ratios.
findings.evidence:
INVENTURE, 10:1 face-value split ex 2021-06-24:
  2021-06-23  close 39.40  volume  2,747,699
  2021-06-24  close  4.55  volume 37,092,018   <- 13x the prior session, purely mechanical

Counting events inside the 60 sessions following a split/bonus ex-date with a known factor:
  vol_x=5:   4,740 of 222,914 events (2.1%)
  vol_x=10:  2,392 of  96,490 events (2.5%), of which 228 sit on the ex-date itself

And the contamination is concentrated in the strongest signals: median vol_ratio for events in a post-split window is 10.11 versus 8.90 for all events.
findings.why_it_inflates: Companies split after the price has risen, so split-artefact 'spikes' are systematically drawn from names in an uptrend. They are over-represented at the strictest threshold (vol_x=10), which is exactly the variant a search would select as the winner. Any future volume-, liquidity- or turnover-based signal built on this query inherits a built-in momentum bias that has nothing to do with the hypothesis being tested.
findings.fix: Compute the volume baseline on split-adjusted volume (raw volume divided by the same cumulative factor used for prices, or equivalently compare turnover against a turnover median, which is share-count invariant). At minimum, exclude sessions within +/- 5 days of any corporate action with a factor, and report how many events that removes.

findings.problem: A symbol is declared 'delisted' purely because its price series stops. That test cannot distinguish a real delisting from a ticker rename, a demerger, or a scheme of arrangement, all of which are common in India and none of which are a bad outcome. The event is then force-exited at an arbitrary date under the mis-aligned benchmark of finding 3.
findings.evidence:
982 of 3,533 INE-prefixed symbols are flagged 'delisted' by this rule (28% of the universe). Of those, 187 have an ISIN that is still trading under a different symbol on the most recent sessions — the company did not die, the ticker changed:
  TATAMOTORS  INE155A01022  series ends 2025-10-23  (demerger)
  MINDAIND    ...           ends 2022-08-04         (renamed UNOMINDA)
  WABCOINDIA, SUNDARMHLD, PAPERPROD, KAVVERITEL, SPICEMOBI, CESCVENT, SHIL, STAMPEDE, MODISNME, IBWSL ...
The delisted count in the shipped results (294 of 2,400 baseline events, 350-392 of 3,000 per volume variant) therefore overstates real delistings by roughly a fifth, and every one of those events is scored on a truncated window.
findings.why_it_inflates: TATAMOTORS is recorded as ceasing to exist in October 2025 at its last traded price, with the index credited a full 24 months of return against it. The archive's central claim — that delisted names are genuinely retained end to end — is only half true: they are retained, but a fifth of them are not delistings, and all of them are mis-benchmarked. Direction depends on which arm holds more renamed names, so it can flatter a strategy as easily as penalise it.
findings.fix: Resolve continuation by ISIN: if the symbol's ISIN still trades under another symbol after the series ends, splice the successor series rather than exiting. Where no successor exists, distinguish a real delisting (verify against the corpactions 'other'/delisting rows) from a data gap, and report the three counts separately in summarise() instead of a single `delisted` column.

findings.line_hint: 180-192 — entry_px taken from adj_open, while bm_entry at 192 is the index CLOSE on the same date
findings.problem: The stock is bought at the entry session's OPEN and the benchmark at that same session's CLOSE. The stock's return therefore includes one extra intraday session that the index return does not, and the size of that extra session differs systematically between the signal arm and the control.
findings.evidence:
Mean open-to-close return on the entry session:
  volume-spike events (3,000):  -0.655%  (median -0.827%)
  random baseline    (2,400):  -0.204%  (median -0.290%)
A systematic -0.45pp differential applied to the signal arm relative to the control, present at every horizon.
findings.why_it_inflates: It is small here and points against the signal, but it is a genuine one-day misalignment between the two legs of the excess-return calculation — the same class of error as the 30% CAGR bug. On a signal with positive day-after drift it would silently credit the strategy with an intraday move the benchmark never had.
findings.fix: Buy the benchmark at the same instant as the stock. Either use the index open on the entry date, or set entry_px to the entry session's close so both legs are close-to-close, and state which convention is in force.

findings.line_hint: 286-292 — the baseline universe query applies no series filter and no minimum-history requirement, unlike find_events at study_volume.py:81-87
findings.problem: The control arm is drawn from a wider universe than the signal arm can ever produce. find_events requires series IN ('EQ','BE') and at least 36 of the prior 60 sessions of history; baseline() requires only isin_code LIKE 'INE%' and turnover on the day, so newly listed instruments and rights entitlements can enter the control but are structurally impossible in the signal.
findings.evidence: Of 2,400 baseline picks, 45 have fewer than 90 days of listed history and 1 is a rights entitlement. The archive holds 228 rights-entitlement symbols (suffix -RE/-RE1/-RE2/-RE3, series 'BE', median life 7 sessions, 363 sessions above the 1cr turnover bar). Zero of them appear in any of the 222,914 vol_x=5 events, because the hist >= 36 requirement excludes them. HERIT-RE reached the baseline outcome table with entry_date == exit_date and was scored 'complete' at all four horizons on a one-day return.
findings.why_it_inflates: Any difference between the arms that comes from universe composition rather than from the signal is attributed to the signal. Here it is under 2% of the control so it does not move the conclusion, but the asymmetry will grow for any signal with a longer formation window (momentum needs 273 sessions), where the control keeps including names the strategy could never have held.
findings.fix: Give baseline() the same universe predicate as the signal being tested — pass the filter in rather than hard-coding a looser one — and exclude non-common-equity instruments (symbols matching -RE[0-9]*$) from the archive's tradeable universe at the source.

findings.problem: The comment says the sample is spread evenly across time rather than truncated, but the stride is computed by integer division, so whenever max_events < found < 2 * max_events the stride collapses to 1 and .head() keeps only the EARLIEST events — the exact truncation the comment claims to avoid.
findings.evidence: With max_events=3000: found=4500 gives step = 4500//3000 = 1, so ev.iloc[::1] is the whole frame and .head(3000) keeps the first 3,000 rows of an ORDER BY date result — every event after roughly the two-thirds point of the archive is discarded. Not triggered at current settings (found ranges 96,490 to 407,224, so step is 32 to 135), which is why it has not shown up; the shipped runs are genuinely spread (218-350 sampled events per year against 13k-26k found per year).
findings.why_it_inflates: A latent trap that fires exactly when a variant is made more selective — the direction any search moves. A rarer signal producing 4,000 events would silently be evaluated only on 2016-2021, and any period-specific effect would be reported as a property of the signal.
findings.fix: Sample without the stride/head combination: ev.sample(n=max_events, random_state=seed) for an unbiased draw, or use np.linspace indices for a genuinely even stride. Assert that the sampled date range and per-year counts match the full population before recording the trial.

findings.line_hint: 41-52 — _truncated_copy executes store.SCHEMA and copies only the prices table
findings.problem: The look-ahead detector physically truncates only `prices`. store.SCHEMA (store.py:19-34) defines nothing but the prices table, so the truncated archive contains no announcements, financials, indices or corpactions at all. The strongest test in the project covers only price-derived strategies.
findings.evidence: store.SCHEMA contains a single CREATE TABLE for prices. leak.py line 46 selects only 'SELECT * FROM prices WHERE date <= ?'. tests/test_leak.py exercises exactly two strategies, both price-only (Leaky and Momentum). The archive's largest and most leak-prone asset — 276,000 announcements carrying both an_dt and trade_date, where an off-by-one between the two is the canonical error — is never subjected to the test. Nor is es.measure() itself, which is the code that actually produced every published number.
findings.why_it_inflates: The project's stated defence against a repeat of the 30% CAGR bug does not extend to the data most likely to cause it. A screen that reads an announcement at an_dt rather than trade_date would pass every test in the repo, because the announcements table is not part of the test at all.
findings.fix: Extend store.SCHEMA (or add a per-table truncation registry) so _truncated_copy reproduces every table with its own asof column — prices.date, announcements.an_dt, financials.broadcast_dt, indices.date, corpactions.ex_date — and add a deliberately leaky announcement strategy to tests/test_leak.py that keys on an_dt instead of trade_date, asserting the detector catches it.

findings.line_hint: 172-178 — `if series is None or series.empty: continue` and `if after.empty: continue`
findings.problem: measure() drops events for two reasons — the symbol has no price history, or there is no session after the signal date — and returns no record of how many it dropped. The second case selectively removes events on a stock's final trading session, which are the worst outcomes in the sample.
findings.evidence: Verified on the shipped baseline: 2,400 picks in, 9,600 outcome rows out, 2,400 events measured, 0 dropped. So this is not currently corrupting results. But the count is invisible: summarise() reports events/complete/scored computed from what survived, so a run that lost 15% of its events at the entry step would print a clean-looking table with no indication anything was lost.
findings.why_it_inflates: Silently dropping an event whose stock stopped trading the next day removes the single worst possible outcome and rebuilds survivorship bias inside the study, which is the disease the docstring says the module exists to cure. It is dormant only because the current universe has no such cases.
findings.fix: Return the drop counts alongside the outcomes and surface them in summarise() as `events_in` versus `events_measured`, so the two numbers must reconcile. For an event on a symbol's last session, record a real outcome (entry impossible, or entry at the signal-day close with immediate delisting) rather than dropping the row.
